2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable (cross-sectional spatial design using secondary data; however, non-trivial missing-data exclusions and imputations occur: >10% of block groups per state on average had low-reliability ACS poverty estimates [CV > 40%] and were excluded, 3.7% of CWS [n = 429] and ~6% of POTWs lacking physical addresses were omitted, and in Florida 27% missing drinking water and 7% missing sewer parcel records required deterministic imputation).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious concern (models adjust for population density, percent rural population, high poverty, and county/state random intercepts, but omit racial/ethnic composition despite extensive theoretical discussion of racialized municipal underbounding, as well as housing age and local soil/topography; furthermore, cross-sectional estimates face reverse causality/simultaneity because states such as Florida and Texas mandate water/sewer service provision prior to annexation, and random intercepts assume orthogonality between county/state unobservables and regressors).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-strong (municipal incorporation status is rigorously operationalized using 2010 Census TIGER/Line and Census of Governments functional and class codes [funcstat, classfp], augmented by 240 m building-footprint rasters [>250 parcels/sq mi] to identify unrecognized unincorporated communities and spatial buffers [480 m for Islands, 1.6 km for Fringes approximating extraterritorial jurisdiction], contextualized with state annexation statutes; tempered by majority-land-area aggregation to block groups, a uniform 1.6 km ETJ proxy across states, and pairing 2010 municipal boundaries with 2018 building footprints).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate-to-serious concern (Tier 2b approximates missing utility boundaries using municipal boundaries [e.g., 28% of MS POTWs], risking differential misclassification mechanically correlated with municipal incorporation status; Tier 3 approximates >1/3 of systems in several states as circular buffers from predicted area regressions; unlocated minor utilities are excluded and effectively coded as unserved; Florida relies on parcel-level imputations; and 2010 Census boundaries/demographics are combined with 2018 building footprints and multi-year utility shapefiles, with mixed block groups assigned a single incorporation status by majority area).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate concern (substantial effort compiled digitized service areas for 96% of active retail CWS and 94% of POTWs across study states, resolving overlapping polygons and EPA SDWIS mailing-address errors; however, reliance on municipal-boundary proxies [Tier 2b], circular radius predictions [Tier 3], parcel-level deterministic imputations in Florida, cross-dataset temporal mismatches, and areal coverage rather than verified household connections introduce heterogeneous measurement error).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Can't tell / Low-to-moderate concern (no pre-registration or pre-analysis plan is reported to rule out selective specification of density/buffer thresholds or covariate sets; however, full results across multiple model specifications with and without county/state random effects and poverty interactions are transparently reported for both sewer and drinking water outcomes, and compiled datasets are deposited in the Harvard Repository).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Some concern (within the nine study states, all 31,383 Census block groups meeting explicit settlement-density criteria were systematically included, but the nine eastern U.S. states were purposively selected—limiting generalizability to western states—and block groups with low-reliability ACS poverty estimates [CV > 40%, >10% of block groups per state on average] as well as minor utilities lacking physical locations were excluded).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: Explicit quantitative and spatial inclusion/exclusion criteria are stated for community grid cells (>250 parcels/sq mi via >5.56 building centroids or >=662 sq m footprint per 240 m cell; excluding zero-population Census blocks, waterbodies, parks, military bases, and polygons <3,035 sq m), utilities (active retail CWS excluding wholesalers; active POTW sewer systems), and ACS poverty reliability (excluding block groups with CV > 40%), although the rationale for selecting the specific nine eastern U.S. states is not explicitly detailed beyond data compilation and representing >25% of the U.S. population.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The 31,383 Census block groups across nine states (Connecticut, Florida, Kentucky, Mississippi, New Jersey, North Carolina, Rhode Island, Texas, and West Virginia) are thoroughly characterized in terms of state annexation/incorporation regimes, population, land area, settlement typologies (Incorporated, Island, Fringe, Outlying), urban/rural distribution, and poverty terciles, with metropolitan case illustrations.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Municipal incorporation status and unincorporated typology (Island, Fringe, Outlying) are systematically derived from official 2010 Census TIGER/Line places, Census of Governments functional/class codes, and Microsoft building footprints, while high poverty (>=20% below Federal poverty line) is restricted to moderate/high-reliability 2008-2012 ACS estimates (CV <= 40%). Minor misclassification risks arise from assigning mixed-jurisdiction block groups via a majority-land-area rule, applying a uniform 1.6 km extraterritorial jurisdiction buffer, and combining 2010 municipal boundaries with 2018 building footprints.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 10-11, 14] Methods (Identifying incorporated and unincorporated communities; Categorization of unincorporated communities; Demographic data)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Standard federal administrative and regulatory definitions were applied across all nine states, including Census of Governments municipal classification codes (funcstat and classfp), Census Bureau block group and urban/rural definitions, EPA SDWIS active retail community water systems, Clean Water Act NPDES publicly-owned treatment works, and the >=20% Federal poverty threshold.

The authors explicitly identify demographic, geographic, environmental, and institutional confounders—including population density, urban/rural population distribution, household poverty, county and state governance/annexation policies, soil and topographic conditions, and historical racial exclusion/municipal underbounding.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 1-2] Introduction; [PDF Pages 9-11] Methods (Negative binomial regression; Categorization of unincorporated communities)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: Multivariable adjustment for population density, percent rural population, and high poverty, along with county- and state-level random intercepts to account for shared governance and environmental context, are explicitly stated. However, important confounders discussed theoretically—most notably block-group racial/ethnic composition, housing age, and within-county soil/topography—are omitted from the regression models, random intercepts do not guard against regressor-effect correlation, and potential reverse causality from statutory annexation service prerequisites is unaddressed.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Although Tier 1 digitized utility boundaries were compiled and expanded via public records requests (covering 96% of CWS and 94% of POTWs), validity and reliability are compromised across substantial subsets by proxy and imputation methods: Tier 2b substitutes municipal boundaries for missing utility service areas (e.g., 28% of MS POTWs), risking differential misclassification mechanically tied to municipal incorporation status; Tier 3 approximates >1/3 of utilities in several states with predicted circular buffers; 3.7% of CWS and ~6% of POTWs lacking physical addresses were excluded (leaving their areas coded as unserved); Florida sewer coverage relied on parcel matching with deterministic imputations for 27% missing water and 7% missing sewer records; and utility/building datasets from ~2018-2021 were overlaid on 2010 block groups without ground-truth validation of approximations.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 11-14] Methods (Centralized infrastructure coverage; Service area boundaries: data quality; Approximated service area boundaries; Florida: sewer service coverage)

domain_ratings.justification: Multilevel negative binomial generalized linear models with a log block-group area offset and county/state random intercepts appropriately handle overdispersed areal count/rate data and nested geographic clustering, with incidence rate ratios properly computed for nonlinear poverty-by-incorporation interactions and model fit compared via AIC and Vuong tests. Nevertheless, the authors acknowledge unmodeled fine-scale spatial autocorrelation across contiguous block groups, which may deflate standard errors.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Allaire et al. (2024) present an ambitious, large-scale analytical cross-sectional spatial regression study of 31,383 Census block groups across nine eastern U.S. states examining how municipal incorporation status (Incorporated vs. Unincorporated Island, Fringe, and Outlying communities) and high poverty (>=20%) relate to the proportion of community land area unserved by centralized sewer and drinking water systems. Methodological strengths include a transparent geospatial protocol using building footprints to capture unincorporated settlements overlooked by Census Designated Places (69% of unincorporated community land), extensive public-records collection to represent 96% of community water systems and 94% of publicly owned treatment works, careful remediation of EPA SDWIS mailing-address geocoding errors, filtering of unreliable ACS poverty estimates (CV <= 40%), and multilevel negative binomial regression with an area offset and county/state random intercepts. Overall methodological concern is rated as 'Some concern' under the JBI Analytical Cross-Sectional Checklist due to three primary limitations: (1) heterogeneous outcome measurement and potential differential misclassification, notably the use of municipal boundaries as proxies for missing utility service boundaries (Tier 2b, e.g., 28% of Mississippi POTWs, which mechanically aligns measured service boundaries with municipal incorporation status), circular buffer approximations for smaller utilities (Tier 3, >1/3 of systems in several states), omission of unlocated minor utilities, deterministic parcel imputations in Florida, and temporal misalignment across 2010 Census geographies, 2018 building footprints, and multi-year utility records; (2) residual confounding and reverse causality, as regression models omit block-group racial/ethnic composition (despite racialized municipal underbounding being a core theoretical mechanism) and cross-sectional associations cannot separate exclusionary governance from state laws (e.g., in Florida and Texas) requiring water/sewer infrastructure prior to annexation; and (3) unmodeled fine-scale spatial autocorrelation across adjacent block groups and majority-area assignment of mixed-jurisdiction block groups.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Quantitative analytical cross-sectional spatial regression study (multilevel negative binomial GLM across 31,383 Census block groups in nine U.S. states)
